Goody-goodies sign surety bonds to bring refugees into Germany, now have to cover all costs until they find a job (Translation in the comments)

Once they were refugee helpers: many German families signed surety bonds to help refugees bring their relatives to Germany. The states supported this practice and told the citizens that the sureties will expire in no longer than a year. The federal government, however, doesn't agree with this promise. The helpers are now faced with the financial ruin.

It's an absurd situation produced by a combination of bad planing, frivolous promises and a lack of communication between the states and the federal government. The backstory: in 2013, before the big wave of refugees from Syria, every German state with the exception of Bayer, started a humanitarian program to reunite the refugees with their families. So it was possible for the relatives of a refugee living in Germany to enter the country.

The prerequisites: the relatives living in Germany bear all the costs for the travel and accommodation of the incoming persons, like flight ticket, bureaucratic fees, rent and other living expenses. Many of the Syrian families could not afford this - and German helpers signed surety bonds. One of the initiatives in the city of Bonn took 19 sureties.

State-aided - right?

Its members signed the sureties for two reasons, explain the founder Christian Osterhaus to the "Welt" (newspaper): "The escape through people smugglers is very dangerous and with the family reunification we are helping them to avoid the dangerous journey through the Mediterranean sea. Furthermore, people coming through the legal way have better and faster integration possibilities".

This is why the state promoted the use of surety by the helpers - and they have to pay nothing at first. This was the promise of prominent politicians like Ralf Jäger (SPD), who assure that the surety will expire as soon as the refugee is granted asylum. This promise was repeated as recently as in April 2015 during a celebration at his ministry.

Without this nobody would have signed surety bonds, says Osterhaus to the newspaper: "According to the promises we only expected the costs of the asylum application". In order to be completely sure, he even consulted with lawyers.

Empty promises

The issue: the promise was made by politicians only at state level. The federal government doesn't agree with them. Now helpers like Osterhaus suddenly get post from the job centers demanding 4 digit payments.

Refugees can demand social help once asylum is granted. The federal government is responsible for the payments, but uses the surety bonds to cover the costs.

This is perfectly fine according to the laws since there is no expiration date for the sureties. The signer of the surety is responsible for covering all the expenses of the corresponding refugee until he finds a job. Because of legal hurdles and given that the refugee must first be integrated, finding a job can take a while. The new integration law set an upper duration of 3 years for surety bonds. Osterhaus will be paying a total of 32,000€ for his two refugees.

Personally, he isn't facing bankruptcy because of this, however, it hits other helpers harder. "Some people signed bonds for five or six refugees", he explains. "If the government really pushes with the payments they will have to file bankruptcy." The government would have his money back and sent a clear signal at the same time: helping refugees is not worth it.
